== Biography ==

Alice is a young girl of curious and questioning temperament. On a drowsy summer afternoon, while sitting by her sister on the bank, she becomes restless and bored with the idle hours. Observing her sister read a book without pictures or conversations, she grows critical of its utility and falls into contemplation about the merits of making a daisy-chain instead.

Her most notable quality is her capacity for wonder and adaptation in the face of extraordinary circumstances. When a White Rabbit with pink eyes runs past her, her curiosity overwhelms her inertia, and she follows the creature down a rabbit-hole into Wonderland. There she undergoes bewildering transformations—growing to nine feet in height, shrinking again, and navigating an increasingly surreal landscape. Throughout these physical metamorphoses, she maintains her composure and pragmatism, particularly her impulse toward kindness: she thinks to herself that she must be kind to those she encounters, "or perhaps they won't walk the way I want to go."

Alice possesses a distinctive blend of politeness and directness. She is eager to engage with the creatures she meets, conversing with them as if they were lifelong acquaintances. She does not shrink from argument or disagreement, notably disputing with the Lory over questions of age and knowledge, and later questioning the Caterpillar about the nature of her own identity. She observes keenly—noting the peculiar appearance of the footmen at the Duchess's house, the curious busywork of the gardeners painting white roses red, and the absurd logistics of a croquet game played with living creatures as implements.

Alice's demeanor in Wonderland is marked by a measured propriety mixed with growing exasperation. She expresses dismay when startled, bows to the conventions of courtesy even when addressing hostile figures, and shows genuine concern for the welfare of those around her—apologizing earnestly when she accidentally upsets the jury-box at the court proceedings. Her thinking is orderly and practical; she reasons through problems methodically, even as the world around her defies all reason.

== Narrative role ==

Alice is a young girl whose curious temperament and willingness to question the absurd world around her drive her through a series of extraordinary encounters. Bored while sitting by her sister on a bank, she becomes transfixed when a White Rabbit with pink eyes runs past her, and follows it down a rabbit-hole into a deep well. During her descent, she contemplates the distance fallen and thinks of her cat Dinah.

Upon reaching the bottom, Alice undergoes a bewildering series of transformations. She grows to nine feet tall, her body becoming disproportionately large and causing her great distress about managing her distant feet. After crying profusely and creating a pool of tears, she finds herself in conversation with a wet party of animals and birds assembled on a bank—the Mouse, the Lory, and others. It seems quite natural to her to talk familiarly with them as if she had known them all her life, though she quarrels with the Lory over the question of age. When the Dodo declares that everybody has won and all must have prizes, Alice distributes comfits from her pocket as rewards.

Mistaken by the White Rabbit for his housemaid, Alice is sent to fetch his gloves and fan from his house. She discovers an unlabeled bottle and drinks from it, growing so rapidly that she becomes trapped in the room with her limbs protruding from the window and chimney. The Rabbit and other animals attempt to retrieve her, sending a creature named Bill down the chimney, whom Alice kicks out violently. Through careful consumption of mushroom pieces from opposite sides, she experiences rapid and disorienting size changes, eventually managing to shrink small enough to re-enter the hall. Using a golden key, she reaches a beautiful garden with flower-beds and fountains.

In the garden, Alice encounters three gardeners painting white roses red, and observes their work with curiosity. When the Queen arrives in procession with soldiers, courtiers, and guests including the White Rabbit, Alice defiantly refuses to lie flat during the procession and speaks boldly when questioned, prompting the Queen to order her beheading. The King intervenes to spare her, and the Queen instead orders the three gardeners' execution. Alice secretly rescues them by hiding them in a flower-pot, after which the Queen invites her to play croquet—a difficult game indeed, with the Queen quarreling and fighting over hedgehogs and repeatedly shouting "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" Alice confides her frustrations about the game to the Cheshire Cat, who appears gradually in the air. She is then escorted by the Queen back to the croquet game, where the Queen executes most of the other players except the King and Alice.

The Queen asks if Alice has seen the Mock Turtle and offers to have him tell his history. Alice meets the Gryphon, who assures her that the Queen never actually executes anyone. The creatures then demand that Alice repeat lessons. She attempts to recite "'Tis the voice of the Sluggard" but it becomes "'Tis the voice of the Lobster" due to her distraction with the dance. She recites another poem about an Owl and Panther sharing a pie, though the creatures grow frustrated with her inability to explain the absurdities. Throughout, she observes the illogical conversations and strange customs of these creatures with growing bewilderment.

At the trial, Alice observes the courtroom proceedings and notes the absurdity of the twelve jurors writing down their names before the trial has begun. When she finally declares the court nothing but a pack of cards and defies the Queen's orders, the card-creatures fly at her and disperse.

== Personality ==

Alice is governed by curiosity and a restless, inquiring mind. She finds herself bored by passivity and drawn to investigation: sitting idle by her sister, she peers into an unillustrated book and questions its worth, and later she stands watching gardeners at their peculiar work, thinking it "a very curious thing" and drawing nearer to observe. This impulse to look, to listen, and to understand drives much of her conduct in Wonderland.

She possesses a rational, argumentative disposition. When the Lory declares itself older and wiser, Alice refuses to accept this claim without evidence, insisting it reveal its age before she will concede the point. She engages in careful observation and reasoning, as when she deduces that the White Rabbit has mistaken her for his housemaid by noting his formal dress and angry tone. Even when confused or displaced, she maintains logical thought.

Alice is capable of both compassion and pragmatism. She thinks kindly toward creatures in distress, resolving to be gentle to her distant feet lest they refuse to obey her, and planning to give them new boots at Christmas. She feels genuine dismay when she upsets the jurymen with her skirt, exclaiming in distress and hastening to help them, her mind racing with the false notion that they must be returned to their box or they will perish. Yet she is also unafraid to defy authority: she does not flinch when the Queen demands her beheading, and she speaks boldly even in the Queen's presence.

Her temperament shows moments of sharp surprise and candid expression. When confronted with sudden or impossible changes, she speaks with wonder and exasperation—"Curiouser and curiouser!"—and admits openly when her composure fails, confessing she has momentarily forgotten proper English. She is easily startled by authority figures and unexpected demands; when the White Rabbit calls to her in an angry tone and orders her away, she flees at once in fright, too frightened even to correct his mistake about her identity.

== Appearance ==

Alice is subject to sudden and dramatic changes in size. From her own point of view, she has grown as large as nine feet tall at times, her body becoming disproportionately large and difficult to manage. She possesses feet distant enough that she contemplates the trouble of reaching them, and a skirt with an edge substantial enough to tip over a jury-box. Her hands are capable and dexterous, suited to hunting for objects and handling tasks with good nature.

== Powers ==

Alice possesses no magical abilities, yet she demonstrates a peculiar susceptibility to the transformative properties of Wonderland. She undergoes remarkable changes in size without apparent cause or comprehension of the mechanism: at one moment she grows to nine feet tall, lamenting "now I'm opening out like the largest telescope that ever was!" At another, she shrinks again, all within the compass of a single day. These metamorphoses are involuntary and distressing to her, yet she endures them with a curious resilience, managing her altered proportions with good-natured effort even as her limbs become distant and unmanageable.

Beyond her susceptibility to Wonderland's peculiar physics, Alice demonstrates an unusual capacity for discourse with creatures of every description. She finds it "quite natural to Alice to find herself talking familiarly" with animals and birds, conversing with them "as if she had known them all her life," despite their bewildering and often contradictory natures. She disputes with the Lory about questions of age and authority, maintains composure in absurd conversations, and shows keen powers of observation—noticing that footmen in livery have "powdered hair that curled all over their heads" and making careful study of the curious gardeners at their work.

== Relationships ==

'''[[White Rabbit]]''' — acquaintance. Alice first noticed the White Rabbit running past her and followed it down the rabbit-hole into Wonderland. She has pursued the creature through halls and passages, though the Rabbit regards her with alarm and has mistaken her for his housemaid Mary Ann.

'''[[Queen]]''' — enemy. The Queen has repeatedly ordered Alice's beheading, crying "Off with her head!" yet Alice has responded with defiance and boldness, silencing the Queen through her refusal to be cowed.

'''[[Dinah]]''' — family. Alice speaks fondly of her cat Dinah and worries that Dinah will miss her greatly while she remains in Wonderland. She wishes Dinah were with her and hopes that Dinah is remembered at tea-time.

'''[[Gryphon]]''' — acquaintance. Alice and the Gryphon have disputed matters of education and knowledge. The Gryphon has questioned her directly about her learning, finding fault with her recitation of poems.

'''[[Caterpillar]]''' — acquaintance. The Caterpillar addressed Alice directly, asking "Who are you?" and expressing skepticism about her claims of changing size. Alice attempted to recite poems for the creature, though her performance was deemed incorrect.

== Trivia ==

* Alice has a habit of observing and evaluating things with particular attention. She noticed that the footmen at the Duchess's house had powdered hair that curled all over their heads, and she made careful judgments about their appearances—considering one a footman by his livery, though by his face alone she would have called him a fish, and another resembled a frog.

* Alice possesses a thoughtful, if sometimes self-centered, sense of responsibility. When she accidentally tipped over a jury-box during the trial, she was seized with dismay and began picking up the jurymen as quickly as she could, recalling that she had once upset a globe of goldfish and fearing the jurymen would die if not returned to the box at once.

* She is prone to spirited debate and will defend her position firmly. When the Lory claimed to be older and therefore must know better, Alice refused to concede without knowing the creature's actual age—a dispute the Lory eventually abandoned by turning sulky.

* Alice demonstrates a capacity for swift practical judgment in uncertain situations. When the White Rabbit mistakenly called her by the name Mary Ann and ordered her to fetch his gloves and fan, she ran off at once without pausing to explain the mistake, later reflecting to herself that he had taken her for his housemaid.

* Her manner with others tends toward kindness mixed with curiosity. She thought it would be "very uncomfortable" for the Dormouse to be used as a cushion at the mad tea-party, yet she felt genuinely curious about the footmen and the events unfolding at the Duchess's house, creeping out to listen and observe.
